distribution: Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans and the Mediterranean; adults commonly use coastal feeding grounds.
depth_context: Illustrative surface-to-routine-resting-depth band. Six nesting females at Ascension Island routinely reached 18–20 m on resting dives; deeper resting dives were rare. Not a maximum diving capability or a global typical range.

distribution: Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans and the Mediterranean, including coastal and oceanic habitats.
depth_context: 26 adult female tracks in the northern Gulf of Mexico spent approximately 80% of their time at 0–30 m. This is a study-specific time-use band, not a species-wide limit.

distribution: Oceanic and coastal waters worldwide, extending into cooler feeding regions.
depth_context: Post-nesting females tracked from Gabon predominantly occupied the upper 200 m. Deep dives also occurred. This is not a maximum diving capability or a measurement for the demo route.

distribution: Tropical Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, often associated with reefs.
depth_context: Adult eastern Pacific hawksbills in Gaos et al. spent nearly all their time in the upper 10 m. Other populations use deeper habitats; this is not a universal range.

distribution: Primarily the Gulf of Mexico and northwestern Atlantic; adults commonly use nearshore habitats.
depth_context: Bottom-associated behaviour of ONE immature turtle in Gullivan Bay, southwest Florida, occurred in 2–3 m water. This narrow case-study range must not be shown as the typical range for the entire species.

distribution: Tropical Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, in coastal and oceanic habitats.
depth_context: Range of individual MEAN maximum dive depths in a northern Australia telemetry study, not a minimum-to-maximum range of individual dives. Deepest recorded dive was 200 ± 20 m.

distribution: Northern Australian waters and adjoining waters of Indonesia and Papua New Guinea; all known breeding sites are in Australia.
depth_context: Surface-to-study-maximum band for inter-nesting females at Curtis Island, Queensland. The same study recorded a maximum of 44 m at Bare Sand Island. These are local observations, not physiological limits.
